sections.heading: ePBS Malicious Payload Testing
sections.summary: Toni reported testing oversized/invalid ePBS payloads on devnet 8; deeper CL-EL interaction analysis needed before Monday's ACDT call.
sections.body:
- Toni has been testing malicious payloads on devnet 8 that appear valid to the CL (below the 10 MB cap) but are invalid on the EL side (blob hash mismatch), filled with 13 max-size transactions doing as many KZG pairings as possible, padded with garbage data to nearly 10 MB.
- The CL forwards these payloads to the EL, which begins executing them; most ELs abort execution early, but Besu had an issue (now fixed) where execution took up to 12 seconds.
- A related attack vector: publishing a very heavy payload (e.g., 300 million gas, above the gas limit) very late in the slot forces the EL to execute it and miss building on top for the next slot.
- Mikhail noted there is also an Engine API dimension related to payloads that take a long time to execute and the CL behavior around it.
- Discussion is ongoing in the Interop Discord channel; Mikhail and Potuz are analyzing the situation. Deeper discussion planned for Monday's ACDT call.
- A proposal by Nico to check minimum gas per transaction ([consensus-specs PR #5802](https://github.com/ethereum/consensus-specs/pull/5802)) was mentioned as a potential mitigation.

sections.heading: Execution Payload Gossip Validation and Block Hash Check
sections.summary: Decision on adding block_hash gossip validation (via RLP or payload root in bid) deferred pending EL decisions on 8037/8038 and Sepolia status.
sections.body:
- Justin Traglia presented [consensus-specs PR #5770](https://github.com/ethereum/consensus-specs/pull/5770), which adds gossip checks to execution payload envelope validation for Glamsterdam, including a controversial execution block_hash check requiring RLP encoding capability in the CL.
- Most CL clients already have a function for computing the execution block hash; Mikhail confirmed all CLs can do the check based on Discord discussions.
- Cayman (Lodestar) argued for the cleaner alternative: adding a payload root field to the bid, avoiding bringing EL commitment machinery into the CL. He agreed to open a PR for this approach after the call.
- Enrico (Teku) said Teku already implements the check using a Besu dependency and has a PR to reuse the same machinery for gossip validation, but changing the bid structure now feels too late.
- Grandine confirmed they already have the block_hash check implemented.
- Potuz noted that adding a root check to the bid would be a hard blocker for future slot-type auctions, since it creates a commitment on transactions that is harder to remove. However, he agreed it is better than doing RLP on the CL.
- Terence raised the question of whether Sepolia is already broken; pk910 noted Sepolia is basically end-of-life and should not block decisions.
- Barnabas emphasized not overcomplicating the CL just for the sake of saving Sepolia; a new testnet can be launched next year.
- Decision deferred to after the ACDT call on Monday, pending clarity on 8037/8038 EL decisions and Sepolia status. A breakout may be organized.

sections.heading: Devcon L1 R&D Workshop Recap
sections.summary: Will summarized the two-day Devcon workshop covering Glamsterdam retro, Hegota planning, and an emergent multi-day PQ/AI urgency discussion.
sections.body:
- The EF protocol cluster organized a two-day workshop before Devcon, as is tradition.
- Day 1 focused on Glamsterdam retro and Hegota planning: volatile frames, devnet planning, 8037 networking breakouts, and integrating AI into the development process. Three rooms were recorded; recordings are being processed.
- Day 2 focused on ISTAR and the PQ roadmap, starting with a presentation from Project 11 (a blockchain-agnostic quantum consultancy group) on migration paths and deadlines for governments and financial institutions.
- Justin Drake presented an updated PQ roadmap based on the Cambridge Post-Quantum Workshop held two weeks prior.
- The Cambridge workshop consensus on Q-Day shifted from 2032 (a year ago) to 2029 (current consensus), reflecting acceleration in AI capabilities and challenges to ECC.
- Discussion during the workshop led to a spontaneous multi-day continuation in "Room 203" at Devcon, with scenario planning, CL/EL breakouts, and exploration of more aggressive fork timelines.
- Justin Drake had previously presented "Mission 2028" with 3 post-Glamsterdam hard forks; the Room 203 discussions explored even more aggressive approaches.
- EF cryptography team members (George Kadianakis, Dmitry Khovratovich, Antonio Sanso, Gottfried Herold) were present on the call for PQ/AI questions.

sections.heading: Post-Quantum / Post-AI Urgency Assessment
sections.summary: Rough consensus emerged around DEFCON 2-3 urgency, with PQ/AI as the collective priority for upcoming forks while avoiding reckless shortcuts.
sections.body:
- Ben Edgington presented a DEFCON-style urgency scale (1-5) to frame the discussion, noting the community has been at DEFCON 4 and may now be at 3 or 2.
- Matthew Keil suggested DEFCON 3 but emphasized planning for DEFCON 2 scenarios proactively.
- Soispoke cautioned against panic reactions, noting no new factual evidence has changed recently, and warned about costs of rushing: losing credibility, restarting scoping, shipping bugs, and the irony of breaking Ethereum while trying to secure it.
- Barnabé Monnot argued both the emergency level and the opportunity/capability to ship PQ have increased dramatically, with stronger cryptographic results, benchmarks, and protocol confidence.
- Fredrik noted AI capabilities are accelerating rapidly and the main concern from lab contacts is crypto breaking through AI sooner than PQ hardware arrives; the migration period for users will be long, so starting early is critical.
- Caspar Schwarz-Schilling (ETH Labs) advocated making PQ/AI the collective primary focus for all post-Glamsterdam forks, arguing it is the least costly approach overall and avoids repeated governance re-evaluation. ETH Labs posted their position on [ETH Magicians](https://ethereum-magicians.org/t/an-ethlabs-view-on-post-quantum-and-post-ai-timelines-pqai27/30351).
  - ETH Labs offered to withdraw Quick Slots (EIP-8198) from Hegota to demonstrate commitment.
- Łukasz Rozmej agreed with prioritization but argued teams should still ship non-conflicting features in parallel rather than abandoning everything.
- Justin Drake reported that the EF is investigating whether cryptographic breaks may have already been found and withheld by AI labs; results (positive or negative) will be made public once investigations conclude in the coming weeks.
- Ben Adams warned against being overly aggressive and entering a "too-many-cooks" situation where timelines don't shorten but less gets shipped overall.
- Vitalik noted in chat: "defcon 2.5 + some of our talent is busy hardening against client bugs = equivalent to defcon 2."
- Ansgar Dietrichs suggested the response should be "full focus but proper diligence" rather than "ship without due diligence," and that the most important decision is whether to make PQ the collective focus.
- Lambda teams (ethrex/ethlambda) stated they view the situation at DEFCON 2.
- Barnabas framed the key question: if we don't start PQ work now (DEFCON 2), we likely won't look at it closely until the next fork, probably a year from now (DEFCON 3).
- No one argued for staying at DEFCON 4 or 5 when asked for contrarian views.
- Hash-based cryptography was discussed as the safest option: Vitalik noted it is the only "single-ingredient" option; Dmitry Khovratovich noted even old hashes like MD4 remain secure if rounds are doubled; George Kadianakis noted hashes are easy to swap and fortify.
- Multiple participants emphasized that client hardening against AI-driven bug discovery is equally important as PQ cryptographic migration.

sections.heading: Hegota Scoping and FOCIL
sections.summary: Hegota scoping is being reopened; FOCIL's compatibility with PQ is the most urgent open question, with no decision made yet.
sections.body:
- Caspar confirmed ETH Labs is withdrawing Quick Slots from Hegota; Barnabé Monnot confirmed this with a link to [his comment](https://github.com/ethereum/pm/issues/2291#issuecomment-6825223023).
- Ansgar outlined concrete implications on the CL side: FOCIL definitely in Hegota at DEFCON 3, likely postponed at DEFCON 2; PQDC at DEFCON 3, choice of PQDC vs PQ Gasper at DEFCON 2; quick slots and small feature EIPs questionable at 3, definitely out at 2.
- Potuz argued scoping should not be based on future features that depend on a roadmap we never commit to; FOCIL with multi-kilobyte ILs is unlikely to work with PQ Gasper at 12-second slots.
- Soispoke argued FOCIL is relatively simple on the CL side, its interactions with frames are conceptually clear, and it should not be framed as a major blocker for PQ. He noted ILs are highly ephemeral (4-slot lifetime, never on-chain) and need not support all transaction types.
- Matthew Keil asked for concrete design questions that need answering before deciding on FOCIL, particularly regarding EL integration complexity with frames.
- Caspar noted FOCIL compatibility with PQ is unclear, and without FOCIL the CL could move independently from the EL (EL ships frames while CL works on PQ consensus).
- Lean F (ethrex) confirmed they have been working on FOCIL and its interaction with frame transactions but see a potential delay to PQ features.
- Vitalik noted in chat that for FOCIL to work for PQ privacy use cases, it would need to support up to 128 kB, and each IL would need an aggregate STARK even post-EIP-8288.
- Ansgar proposed that the FOCIL decision (confirm for Hegota or postpone) be made at the call in 2 weeks, not today.
- Toni Wahrstätter argued the focus should be on shipping frames on the EL side first, since the CL PQ transition is instant but the EL transition requires user migration, hardware changes, etc.
- Barnabé Monnot gave his view: FOCIL + quick slots are fine for DEFCON 3 / end-2028 delivery with DC, but neither is fine for shipping end-2027 with PQ Gasper.

sections.heading: PQ Gasper vs. PQ Decoupled Consensus
sections.summary: BLS-only decoupled consensus is dead; PQ Gasper should be explored first but may prove infeasible, requiring a fallback to PQ decoupled consensus.
sections.body:
- Justin Traglia proposed spending a few weeks working on PQ Gasper before seriously considering PQDC, noting most PQ Gasper work is also needed for PQDC.
- Mikhail Kalinin cautioned that assessing PQ Gasper feasibility requires deep work on aggregation bandwidth, compute, and attestation pool changes; a few weeks may not yield strong evidence, and switching to PQDC mid-process is a real possibility.
- Potuz agreed with Mikhail but emphasized DC specifications should already target the PQ world, since shipping BLS DC first and then moving to PQ is no longer viable.
- Ben Edgington declared BLS decoupled consensus is dead as an outcome of last week's discussions; any DC work must target PQ from the start.
- Mikhail noted that non-finality periods, already hard with BLS Gasper, would be even worse with PQ Gasper, while PQDC should handle them much better.
- Yann Vonlanthen said PQ DC is close to having a stable protocol but still needs spec work; he shared a [write-up on avenues for PQ Gasper](https://notes.ethereum.org/_rGnW7YuRWurwyA8zFhsog).
- Francesco noted the main thing needing hard evidence is signature aggregation, which is required regardless of Gasper or DC path and should be prioritized heavily.
- Ben Edgington suggested keeping PQ Gasper as a quick-deploy fallback while pursuing PQ DC as the primary path.
- Kamil Salakhiev noted his simulations show 12-second slots can be maintained with PQ signatures.
- Networking was identified by multiple participants as the biggest unknown; Csaba offered to help with P2P questions and referenced [SEACAST](https://notes.ethereum.org/@cskiraly/seacast) work on large message propagation.

sections.heading: LeanVM Readiness and Formal Verification
sections.summary: LeanVM targets production readiness in January 2027 with formal audits starting February 1; client devs need clearer interfaces and evaluation processes.
sections.body:
- Tom Wambsgans confirmed the team is working "extremely hard" to have LeanVM ready in a few months, meaning production-ready (not just testing-ready).
  - Currently only the spec and the Rust verifier have formal verification; the Rust prover does not yet.
- Justin Drake stated the internal goal is production readiness in January, with formal audits kicking off February 1. The team is still working through theoretical issues related to recursion that make the trusted codebase more complicated than desired.
  - For simpler primitives (LeanSPHINCS, LeanXMSS), an ultra-minimal trusted codebase has already been achieved.
  - The goal is hundreds to low-thousands of Lean4 lines of code in the trusted codebase.
- George Kadianakis emphasized that LeanVM is a very large cryptographic black box, bigger than what client devs are used to, and called for establishing guidelines and processes for how client devs interact with and evaluate it.
  - He stressed the need to define what "ready" means beyond the developers declaring it ready, including the audit surface, FV architecture, and real-world usage assumptions.
- Potuz called for multiple implementations of LeanVM, arguing formal verification is "irrelevant if I can crash the binary."
- Pawan Dhananjay questioned whether formal verification guarantees no bugs, asking what happens if conditions are missed when specifying constraints.
- Dima Gusakov offered a hot take that formal verification is overrated; multiple participants agreed it should not be marketed as a silver bullet.
- George Kadianakis countered that figuring out how to make FV work effectively is essential for long-term internet security in the AI era, and that learning to communicate FV's specific guarantees is critical.
- Vitalik noted in chat that the LeanVM line-of-code count should ultimately include the Lean verifier itself.
- Discussion on where LeanVM productization conversations are happening: Discord channels in the R&D server were referenced.

sections.heading: PQ Networking and TLS
sections.summary: ~80% of CL network already uses hybrid PQ TLS; Felix is working on broader PQ networking including node identities and discovery.
sections.body:
- Matthew Keil raised the question of post-quantum TLS readiness.
- Kamil Salakhiev reported that approximately 80% of the CL network already uses hybrid PQ key exchange via GoLibP2P; he submitted a PR for rust-libp2p as well.
- PQ TLS on the networking side is less consensus-critical but still important, primarily for harvest-now-decrypt-later attacks.
- Felix (Geth) confirmed he is working on PQ conversion for the networking layer beyond just TLS configuration, including node identities and the discovery protocol. He plans to present on this soon.
- EL networking PQ status may differ from CL and needs further attention.

sections.heading: PQ Material Registration EIP (EIP-8483)
sections.summary: EIP-8483 (PQ material registration) was accepted as PFI for Hegota; no objections raised.
sections.body:
- Justin Traglia proposed [EIP-8483](https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/pull/12609) for PFI into Hegota, with a corresponding [consensus-specs PR #5809](https://github.com/ethereum/consensus-specs/pull/5809).
- The EIP allows validators and builders to register PQ keys ahead of a future fork by introducing two new execution request types.
- Registration data is opaque, not locking into a particular signature scheme; re-registration is possible if the scheme changes.
- System contracts can be deployed on the EL within weeks (no fork needed), allowing registration to begin as soon as the signature scheme is finalized.
- At the Hegota fork, the CL would begin consuming queued registrations from the EL into the Beacon state.
- Potuz emphasized the urgent part is agreeing on the design, auditing the contract, and deploying it so the community can start registering; the fork part itself is simple.
- Dima Gusakov (Lido) asked about the risk of registering material that becomes "trash" if the scheme changes; Potuz and Traglia clarified that a new system contract could be deployed if needed.
- Barnabas asked about Beacon state size impact; Potuz estimated ~40 MB for 1 million validators, noting the current state is ~400 MB, and the data is consumed and dropped after the PQ transition fork.
- Kevaundray Wedderburn noted the PQ registry should be in Hegota and highlighted related EIPs: EIP-8151 (disable legacy ecrecover) and EIP-8298 (setcodefrom) for EOA upgrades.
- No objections to PFI; Ben Edgington confirmed the EIP is accepted as PFI, with CFI to be considered at a future call.

sections.heading: Quick Slots DFI and Remaining Hegota EIPs
sections.summary: Quick Slots (EIP-8198) moved from CFI to DFI for Hegota; discussion of other CFI'd EIPs deferred to the next call.
sections.body:
- Caspar Schwarz-Schilling (ETH Labs), as champion of EIP-8198 (Quick Slots), proposed to DFI it from Hegota to make room for PQ priorities.
- Barnabé Monnot, as co-champion, did not object.
- No objections raised; Quick Slots moved from CFI to DFI.
- Soispoke requested that the other CFI'd Hegota EIPs also be discussed; Ben Edgington confirmed this will happen at a future call, not today.
- Ansgar urged that the quick slots sacrifice not be in vain and that the freed capacity actually accelerate PQ work.

sections.heading: Staged PQ Rollout Proposal and Next Steps
sections.summary: Saulius proposed keeping BLS alongside new PQ cryptography for a staged rollout; next call is November 26 (Thanksgiving) and will proceed as scheduled.
sections.body:
- Saulius proposed a staged rollout approach: keep BLS together with new PQ cryptography initially, with ECC retaining authority in some areas (especially aggregate signatures) while LeanVM is refined at mainnet scale.
  - This approach would allow testing and hardening LeanVM without putting Ethereum at risk before PQ/AI day arrives.
  - George Kadianakis acknowledged the incrementalism argument but raised concerns about combiner code bugs reducing security, citing recent CVEs in hybrid cryptographic implementations.
- New post-quantum channels have been created on the R&D Discord for ongoing CL and EL discussions.
- The next call on November 26 (US Thanksgiving) will proceed as scheduled; irrevocable decisions will be avoided if key people are absent.
- Ben Edgington committed to processing the transcript and finding ways forward for future calls.
- Barnabas asked about scoping for the next devnet; Ben said it is too early given no decisions have been made yet.
